newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium condemns Zaire military dictatorship.
newsitem.headline: Belgium condemns Zaire military dictatorship.

text.p: Belgium on Thursday condemned Zaire's appointment of a general as prime minister in its former colony, saying the central African nation was now in the hands of a military dictatorship.

The new government was a "military dictatorship revisited", with a military man as prime minister and the parliament thrown aside, Belgian Foreign Minister Erik Derycke told a news conference on recent developments in Zaire.

Ailing president Mobutu Sese Seko, who has ruled Zaire for 32 years, on Wednesday named General Likulia Bolongo as prime minister in place of Mobutu's long-time rival Etienne Tshisekedi, appointed only a week before.
Derycke likened the current political situation in Zaire to events which led to Mobutu coming to power in 1965.

"President Mobutu could...play a positive role by giving negotiated political solutions a chance for the current crisis. But it seems that President Mobutu, with his coup d'etat, has returned to the point he started out at more than 30 years ago," Derycke said in a statement issued at the news conference.

"He clings on desperately to power, and counts on the support of the DSP and soldiers of the FAZ which fled to Kinshasa and which, it seems, pose the biggest danger for Belgians," the statement added.
The DSP is Mobutu's presidential guard, made up of elite and well-paid troops. The FAZ is Zaire's regular army, which has a reputation for being disorganised, undisciplined and badly paid.

Echoing recent comments by the United States, Derycke reiterated that "politically, the page of Mobutuism was turned over some time ago", but it was up to the people of Zaire to answer the question of whether the veteran ruler, who is suffering from cancer, should resign.
On Wednesday the United States signalled its desire to see Mobutu step down, saying the time for dictatorship was over.

Derycke said talks between Belgium and rebel leader Laurent Kabila, whose forces control about a third of the country after months of fighting, did not constitute a formal recognition of Mobutu's opponent.
"Kabila makes declarations - we have to see if he does what he says he will," Derycke said.
He said Belgium had always worked for the respect of the "basic principles" of Zaire's transition to democracy and eventual elections.

But with the resignation of Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo in March, constitutional arrangements for the period of transition had been violated. Ensuing events had "completely hollowed out" these basic principles of transition, he added.
On the safety of Belgians in Zaire -- 1,519 are in the capital Kinshasa, and 748 in the mineral-rich Shaba province -- Derycke said the government was constantly watching the situation.
The Belgian military currently has 700 people in the region, including 550 paratroops who are standing by to evacuate the nationals if necessary.
